item.title: World Bank chief warns diesel, fertilizer and El Niño pressures are building at once
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrea Shalal BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth. The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held ‌outside of Washington for the first time in three years. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters during a tour of the 300,000 square-meter Queen Sirikit National Convention Center on Sunday evening that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the ‌last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023. SEVERAL FINANCE MINISTERS STAYING AWAY Notably absent will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16. Several other ​finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said. Bessent's decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the U.S. leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion and the U.S. move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court. World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring prices for diesel, rising fertilizer prices and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are all hitting at once. RELEASE OF RESERVES Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, ‌who is keen to see lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party ⁠lose control of Congress. Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of U.S. sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of ⁠oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices. Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination ... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months." RISING DEBT IMF chief Georgieva issued a similar warning in ​her ​traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings last week, telling the audience: "Winter is coming." The IMF has signaled little change in its forecast for 3% global growth in 2026 and ​may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in ‌its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports. IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability. One huge headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030. Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries. EMERGING MARKET CONCERNS Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400 billion in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue on average. Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt ‌service payments for the poorest countries, but there is little appetite for such action now, according to diplomats from G20 countries, who said high debt levels and political ​pressures posed bigger hurdles this time. Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper reforms as a condition for approving ​lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures. "Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going ​high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse." Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting ‌public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young. The IMF ​risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many ​developing countries. "As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said. SECURITY AND FINANCE Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to global travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports. The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people in Israel, followed by Israel's bombardment of Gaza that killed more than ​74,000 people and devastated cities throughout the Palestinian area. Three years later, the linkage between national security and international finance ‌is clear, although finance officials at the time had dismissed the Hamas attack as not being an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council. "Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing ​with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago." Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive ​and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to." (Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Dan Burns and Andrea Ricci) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://ca.news.yahoo.com/middle-east-war-high-debt-040251376.html

item.title: Arizona's GOP keeps embracing election deniers who lose. It could happen again.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Election Day 2020 was fast approaching, and Alexander Kolodin wanted a spot inside the Arizona Republican Party's war room. Kolodin, an attorney who had lost a GOP primary for the state Senate that summer, was seen as something of a gadfly by some in the state GOP and hardly seen at all by others. But the Republicans running the show allowed him into an auxiliary war room on another floor of the hotel, distanced from the real action, one party leader recalled. People there "could say they were in the war room," he said. "If we needed something, then we'd call." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Kolodin didn't wait to be summoned. On Election Day, complaints began flooding in about ballots marked with Sharpie markers. Soon, supporters of President Donald Trump were blaming Sharpies for what looked like a loss in Arizona. The Arizona Republican Party had investigated the matter and determined that Sharpies had not in fact caused problems. So its leaders were surprised when they learned that Kolodin was filing a lawsuit demanding that voters who used Sharpies be given a chance to vote again. The suit was filed the day after the election, the first of several challenges Kolodin championed over the 2020 results. Each failed in court, and they led to sanctions from the state bar association. But Kolodin's embrace of these claims catapulted him from a little-known attorney who badly lost his first campaign for office to a leading figure in Arizona politics and this year's Republican nominee for secretary of state. If he wins, he will be responsible for running the state's elections in 2028, when Arizona is expected to once again be a battleground in the presidential and Senate contests. Other election conspiracy theorists hold high office, but a victory here would mark the first time someone actively involved in attempting to subvert election results would be elected to run a state's elections. Arizona was a reliably Republican state just a decade ago, and then seen as a competitive battleground. But in recent years, the state GOP has repeatedly nominated candidates who have promoted Trump's false claims, only to see them lose in the general election. That includes Blake Master, who lost a Senate race in 2022, and Kari Lake, who lost races for governor in 2022 and Senate in 2024, even as Trump won the state. This fall, besides Kolodin, two other Republicans who acted to subvert the 2020 election results are also on the ballot: Andy Biggs for governor and Warren Petersen for attorney general. Some in the party predict a wipeout is coming and worry Democrats will consolidate and expand their power for years to come if Republicans continue this pattern. "The election denialists have dominated this party for six years," said one GOP strategist. "If we keep doing this, we will keep losing." Kolodin is not the only person who has advanced the lie that the 2020 election was stolen and is now running to oversee elections in a presidential battleground state. In Nevada, former state lawmaker Jim Marchant, the GOP nominee for secretary of state, claimed that both he and Trump were victims of election fraud in 2020 and says being called an election denier is a "badge of honor." In a recent interview, Anthony Forlini, Michigan's GOP nominee for secretary of state, wouldn't say who won the presidential election in 2020. "Everyone wants to trip up people on that whole question," he said. In Arizona, endorsing and promoting Trump's conspiracy theories were essential to Kolodin's rise. They brought him to the center of the action, drew admirers in the GOP base and won allies in powerful places. "Alex definitely stepped up when there were very few who could or would," said Tyler Bowyer, CEO of Turning Point USA. "He easily could have been, 'Nah, I'm not going to help.' No one would know who he was and he certainly wouldn't be running for secretary of state now." The cases increased Kolodin's public profile, but it came with a price, said Tyler Montague, president of the Arizona Public Integrity Alliance, a conservative think tank, who has known Kolodin for more than a decade and sometimes worked with him. "He found a path to notoriety and surrendered some of his political thinking to Trump, and that combination led him to where he's at," he said. "It's a cultlike mentality - uncritical acceptance of what the leader says. It's hard for him to get out of it because it's also the source of his status." After fighting for Trump following his 2020 loss, Kolodin was elected to the Arizona House in 2022. There, he earned a reputation as a fighter for ultraconservative principles, but also as an obstructionist who has incensed fellow Republicans as well as Democrats. Two GOP committee chairmen asked for him to be removed from their committees, three people familiar with the situation said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss a personnel matter. Kolodin did not respond to requests for comment or to a list of detailed questions. In other interviews, he has emphasized his support for election integrity, attacked his opponent's record and tried to downplay the events of 2020. "Election integrity has become the defining civil rights issue of our time," he wrote in a post on X thanking Trump for his endorsement. "We must protect the sanctity of every lawful vote, and we must restore confidence in our elections for every lawful voter, regardless of political party." Losses fuel a rising star Kolodin was raised in Arizona and returned to the state after earning a law degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 2013. He set up his own small law practice, taking a series of cases where he challenged government and election procedures, often on hot-button topics of public interest that landed in the news. Among them: He demanded public records in a sports arena deal. He tried to kill mask requirements in a public school district during the pandemic. And he worked to kick a congressional candidate off the ballot because of an error on her nominating petitions. Kolodin made his first run for political office in 2020, mounting a mostly self-funded primary campaign against a Republican incumbent for a state Senate seat. During that campaign, his opponent latched on to Kolodin's involvement in a 2014 defamation lawsuit where he represented a liberal activist who had collected and mailed a huge pile of filled-out ballots. Kolodin lost the case, and also badly lost the GOP primary. But he continued his work on election issues. That fall, he scored a victory in a dispute with Adrian Fontes, who at the time was running elections in Maricopa County, home to Phoenix and the state's largest county. Fontes had told voters that if they made a mistake marking their ballot, they could cross it out and fill in the proper oval. Kolodin's suit argued that this would open the door to allowing people who handle ballots to change votes after the fact. His suit forced a reversal by Fontes, a Democrat who is the current secretary of state and Kolodin's opponent this fall. But when Election Day arrived, his profile began to climb with his Sharpie lawsuit. The allegations, first voiced in remote corners of Twitter, were soon amplified by conservative mega-voices such as Charlie Kirk of Turning Point USA. By 10 a.m. the next day, there were 1,200 tweets per minute on Sharpies, one analysis found. Kolodin asked Montague, the conservative think tank president, if he would be a plaintiff in his Sharpie suit, Montague said. He declined, telling Kolodin there was nothing to these claims. The rumor was based on concerns that using a Sharpie marker would invalidate a ballot because the ink could bleed through and interfere with ballot marks on the other side of the paper. In fact, as the state GOP had discovered, the columns on the other side of the paper were aligned so that any bleed through would not impact other votes. Nonetheless, Kolodin "charged forward," Montague recalled. "He seemed to genuinely believe in the various conspiracy theories going on." One Republican attorney active in the party said Kolodin pursued the suit despite widespread opposition among Republican strategists in D.C. and Arizona. "It felt like he was trying to elbow his way into the conversation and, frankly, the limelight," he said. The case was quickly dismissed, but within weeks, Kolodin was back with another, more sweeping lawsuit, demanding that the election results be set aside due to "massive election fraud." The suit - one of several filed in states Joe Biden won - was conceived by national figures including Trump ally Sidney Powell, who promised these challenges would "release the kraken" and prove Trump actually won the election. She needed an attorney to carry the case, but no prominent Arizona election lawyer, including those who had worked for the Trump campaign and the Republican Party, would take the case, said three people familiar with the conversations inside GOP circles. Kolodin stepped in. "Most of the Republican attorneys saw the need to be as far away from this dumpster fire as you could possible get," said one of these people. "Were you to continue to pursue these cases you could be jeopardizing your law license." A federal judge found the allegations "sorely wanting of relevant or reliable evidence" and in December 2020, dismissed the case. Despite the courtroom setbacks, Kolodin was establishing himself as Arizona's go-to attorney when someone wanted to challenge election results. He represented Cyber Ninjas, which in 2021 ran a chaotic audit of 2020 ballots in Maricopa County (and ultimately found Biden's margin slightly bigger than official results indicated). In 2022, he represented a group that monitored ballot drop boxes and filmed people voting, claiming to be hunting for fraud. And his client list included people who falsely presented themselves as 2020 electors. In 2023, the State Bar of Arizona cited three lawsuits Kolodin filed, including the Sharpie suit, as it formally admonished him for violating his duty to the legal profession, the legal system and the public. The state bar sentenced him to 18 months of probation and required him to take five legal ethics courses. But while Kolodin was accumulating one loss after the next, his public profile was rising. In 2022, he again ran for the legislature, seeking a House seat representing Scottsdale, a suburb of Phoenix. His campaign material highlighted his role in many of these actions. And unlike in summer 2020, this time he won. 'Outrageous lies' Kolodin immediately made his mark in the Capitol, irritating people in both parties with unpredictable personal and legislative behavior, according to current and former lawmakers and others familiar with the situation. He became known for filing voluminous numbers of bills - 74 last year - and also for a proposal last year that would bar any legislator from introducing more than 10 bills per year. He backed a repeal of the ban on machine guns, silencers, sawed-off shotguns and pipe bombs. He was the only legislator of either party to vote against a "stolen valor" bill making it a crime to impersonate a veteran. (He said it would criminalize alleged lies by politicians, setting a dangerous precedent.) Several current and former GOP lawmakers described him as disruptive, unwilling to work with others and insistent on having things his way. Last year, he called any legislator, including some Republicans, who supported a particular version of a budget bill "an enemy of the people of Arizona." "He says things out loud that are nonsensical - objecting to motions, attempting to change procedure in a nonsensical way, outbursts in a heated debate on the floor," said one Republican who worked closely with Kolodin. His style, he said, is to "fly off the handle" and "shoot from the hip." On the campaign trail, Kolodin touts bipartisan successes, and in 2024, he helped reach a bipartisan elections reform package, which aligned post-election timelines for steps such as certification with new federal deadlines. But last year, he blew up chances for a bipartisan agreement with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs's office on another elections measure by insisting on elements that the governor would never agree to - such as requirements making mail voting harder - and being unwilling to compromise, according to two people involved in the process. "He has particular views on certain issues and it's challenging to reason with him or find common ground," said Bo Dul, an Arizona election attorney who served as general counsel to Hobbs. "Often, those views are not grounded in fact or how election administration actually works and, as a result, he would often insist on positions that are just nonstarters." No deal was reached. Instead, the GOP legislature voted to put its proposal before voters this fall. If approved, it would, among other things, require mail-in voters - who make up about 80 percent of all voters in the state - to show identification. It's unclear how or where people voting by mail would be able to show ID. Kolodin has bemoaned failure to advance another election priority: requiring every voter to repeatedly verify their address to vote by mail. In an interview last year, he said that this reform could have helped increase Republican vote share in Arizona. "It could have flipped this state red for a generation. So I was just so incredibly disappointed to see it get killed," he told "The Jeff Oravits Show." Kolodin's panache for irritating his party and for advancing Trump's unfounded claims collided when a group of Arizona Republicans was criminally investigated, and then charged with conspiracy and fraud, for declaring themselves to be the state's representatives to the electoral college in 2020 when Biden actually won Arizona. In 2024, Kolodin, who represented some of these so-called fake electors, argued that the Arizona Republican Party's insurance policy should cover some of the electors' legal fees. He wrote the company that these people were officials of the Arizona Republican Party, according to a letter viewed by The Washington Post. The insurance company wound up paying out the policy's $1 million maximum toward their legal defense, documents show, some of which went to a law firm where Kolodin worked. In January 2026, then-Arizona Republican Party Chairwoman Gina Swoboda informed the party's executive committee that he had done this without consulting her or other party officers and that the result was a 10-fold hike in premiums. "We became aware of this matter in October 2025 when we inquired why our renewal premium was so high," she wrote. She said the party then made the "difficult but necessary decision" to drop coverage for 2026. That meant the officers of the party were vulnerable if they faced damages claims or lawsuits. This summer, Kolodin easily won the GOP primary for secretary of state, beating Swoboda, who had left her position as party chair earlier this year. He is running on election integrity, promising to implement "robust security protocols" and restore confidence in the elections system. But some in his party worry Kolodin's history of questioning election results could harm Republicans. "He is making outrageous lies about very important things related to the office that he is seeking," said Ken Bennett, a former Republican secretary of state and state senator in Arizona. "As long as the Republican Party nominates people who are too far to the right of the mainstream ... those nominees are going to have trouble in the general election," Bennett said of Kolodin. The events of 2020 loom large in Kolodin's race. During a spirited "candidates in conversation" on Arizona public television with his opponent, Kolodin was asked directly if he was an "election denier." "That's absurd," he replied. "I have one of the greatest bipartisan track records of working on elections issues of anybody in recent Arizona history." Pressed again as to whether he was an election denier, Kolodin answered, "No." Followed by reporters into the hallway after the event, he was asked directly if Trump won Arizona in 2020. "I think I answered that question," Kolodin replied. Asked again, Kolodin said, "Look, Joe Biden was the president. Congress said that Joe Biden won. Congress called the race." As for who won Arizona, Kolodin refused to say, asserting that he had already answered the question. After about a minute of this back and forth, the elevator arrived and Kolodin stepped in. Reporters kept pressing: Was the ballot count in Maricopa County accurate? "It's time for us to go," Kolodin replied. He insisted again that he had already answered, and the elevator doors closed. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/arizona-gop-keeps-embracing-election-100000677.html

item.title: Newsom typically relishes battling Trump — except on undocumented students
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Gavin Newsom has rarely shied away from a fight with Donald Trump, especially over immigration. He didn’t hesitate last year to sign into law a ban on federal immigration agents wearing masks in the state. And when he put his name on a package of legislation this year further clamping down on immigration enforcement, he said he was doing so to “push back on Trump’s Orwellian immigrant tactics.” But when it came to a bill that would have required the state’s public universities and community colleges to make undocumented immigrant students eligible for campus employment, Newsom balked. Trump officials, he wrote in a message explaining his veto last month, are “quick to wreak destruction for political spectacle.” The risk of them seeking retribution against the schools was too great. Newsom’s decision to avoid confrontation prolongs a yearslong student-led push to persuade skeptical university officials to enact a first-in-the-nation policy that would benefit the roughly 60,000 undocumented students enrolled in the three school systems. And it has deflated immigrant rights activists in his home state ahead of Newsom's likely presidential run. “There’s disappointment that on this issue, the governor hasn't been willing to take a risk for a very important part of the California population,” said Maria Blanco, the former executive director of the UC Immigrant Legal Services Center. “Even in a progressive state like California, immigration sometimes still continues to be this third rail, especially if you're running for president.” The governor’s unwillingness to force the issue with Trump stemmed, at least in part, from what he said in his veto message was a concern that the hiring requirement wouldn’t hold up under legal scrutiny since federal law prohibits employers from hiring undocumented workers. Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Newsom referred to the governor’s veto message. Advocates for the idea that students living in the country illegally should be permitted to work campus jobs have relied heavily on a legal theory a group of UCLA law professors published in 2022 that argued the federal ban doesn’t apply to state agencies. The theory was enough to spur discussion among the UC Board of Regents, which considered implementing a policy allowing the hires, but ultimately punted on the idea in 2024. Rich Leib, the chair of the regents at the time who had signaled support for hiring undocumented students, said that enthusiasm on the board waned after three "established" law firms said they would not defend the university if its policy was challenged in court. With a second Trump term looming, Leib said a majority of the regents, including him, decided the timing was not right to challenge an administration that could be hostile to immigrants and voted to table the issue. They were particularly concerned, he said, about the possibility that immigration officials might be able to gain access to personal data about undocumented students on the university payroll. “It was the most emotional experience I had as a regent because it brought you to people who were directly negatively affected by it,” Leib said, referring to students who protested at the board meeting following the vote to shelve the plan. “These are people who have done really well their whole lives. They worked really hard to get where they did, and now you're telling them they can't get a job.” Joel Raznick, a regent emeritus who also voted for the delay, said that the possibility of Trump returning to the White House was “certainly on my mind.” Raznick, who emphasized he was not speaking on behalf of the UC, said he had been concerned about the possibility the Trump administration would respond to the hiring policy by cutting federal funding to the university – a tactic it has used in other fights with the UC – and that undocumented students could be “readily identified and deported.” “I thought that we were doing a better service for undocumented students at that moment by preserving the university's ability to operate,” Raznick said. “Because those risks are real, as we now know.” Anna Markowitz, president of the UCLA Faculty Association, which advocated for the hiring policy, pushed back on that rationale. “Who are we allowing to suffer by claiming that we’re saving the institution?” she asked. Omar Rodriguez, a spokesperson for the UC, said that the university’s “evaluation of this important issue is ongoing.” He pointed out that the UC remained neutral on the bill Newsom vetoed. “UC has been a leader in supporting undocumented students, who are vital members of the UC community and make significant contributions to our economy and society as scholars, researchers, and future leaders,” Rodriguez said. Along with the UC, the legislation would have applied to the California State University and community college systems. In statements, spokespeople for both systems said they also did not come out for or against the bill and support undocumented students while complying with state and federal laws. Immigration advocates criticize Newsom and the regents for what they see as their overly cautious approach. Having a law on the books, they argue, would provide a layer of protection for the school systems if they were to have a policy allowing undocumented students to work on campus. They also point to a ruling in a state appeals court last year that found the UC’s adherence to federal law forbidding employment was discriminatory. The ruling stated that the university could not rely on fear of federal retaliation as a reason for not adopting a more permissive stance, and ordered it to “reconsider its policy based on proper criteria.” “They're really caught in between a rock and a hard place,” said Ahilan Arulanantham, a UCLA law professor who helped write the 2022 legal theory. “They have to comply with the state court decision, and they're not going to get the benefit of any California legislation protecting them from above.” The ruling, though, did not require the university to change its policy and did not include a deadline for the UC to comply. “Large institutions tend to be risk adverse,” Blanco said. “And I don't think this is a climate where the UC would affirmatively go do this and then wait to be sued.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/11/newsom-veto-student-jobs-trump-01113178

item.title: 6 senators call for White House to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law." Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. item.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, but Zelensky says it's news to him
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.” Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to continue their aerial attacks on each other’s energy facilities. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include. Zelenskyy told Axios that he knew nothing about a ceasefire deal. “But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree,” Zelenskyy said, according to Axios. “If President Trump negotiated it with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.” NBC News has reached out to Zelenskyy’s office for further comment. It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling. The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that. Smoke rises from Gazprom Neft's Moscow oil refinery as seen from Dzerzhinsky, in the Moscow region, last month. (AFP via Getty Images) After strong criticism from Zelenskyy, Trump said Saturday: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals.” Trump has sought to blame the Ukraine conflict, rather than his own assault on Iran, for a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices to record highs since the U.S. launched the Middle East war in February. Zelenskyy reiterated Sunday that he was ready to halt strikes on Russian refineries if the Kremlin halts its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. “We are ready for energy ceasefire, not to attack energy — both sides,” he said in interview on ABC News’ “This Week.” He added that if Russia wants an energy ceasefire, “we are open for this.” “Don’t attack us,” he said. “Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel.” The Ukrainian president also told ABC News he would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to ​change who is ​leading Ukraine. He ⁠said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel ​prices “when everybody in the world understands [that] ​because ⁠of the war in [the] Middle East, the prices are rising.” Zelenskyy was also asked on ABC News why Trump and Elon Musk blamed the Ukrainian president for the war’s continuation. “Because these people can’t find a key how to stop Putin, because it’s more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others, because it’s more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine,” he responded, pointing to how the war in Iran was leading to higher fuel prices. item.title: U.K. PM Burnham says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew MacAskill LONDON, Oct 11 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, as he warned voters in France and ‌Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics. Burnham, who took over as Britain's ‌leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, ​is the first British prime minister to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago. "I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I've had the clear answer that yes, there was," Burnham ‌said in an interview with ⁠The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday. Burnham did not spell out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no ⁠details on what evidence this statement was based. The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia has previously denied meddling in the Brexit vote, casting Britain as ​gripped by ​anti-Russian hysteria. Burnham's comments mark a departure from those ​of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, ‌who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum. Britons voted 52%-48% to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since World War Two. Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to disrupt their politics. "I mean, these things are ‌important now to put clearly on the record, and ​I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand ​that some of this politics is ​instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said. Britain's government failed to establish ‌whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum ​on membership of the ​EU, according to a report by parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee in 2020. The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, in which ​voters rejected independence. Burnham last month ‌said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the ​next general election, reopening the country’s divisive debate on its relationship with ​the continent. (Reporting by Andrew MacAskillEditing by Alexandra Hudson) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/uk-pm-burnham-says-russia-165702257.html

item.title: Saudi authorities say King Fahd International Airport in Dammam has been attacked
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people , the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others. Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday’s missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday. The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also had been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back. Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts. “There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference. He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details. Houthis have targeted Saudi air, military and oil facilities Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom’s east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday. The rebels again warned “all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ​travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our ​forces.” Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods. The dead in the airport attack included several nationalities Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday’s attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant for Saudi airline Flynas identified as Azza Ramzy, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother who had been living in Saudi Arabia, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Iran can use the Houthis to pressure a key US ally Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now, they are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels say they have now imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia. Fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has attacked ships. Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.” ___ A previous version of this report has been corrected to show that the Egyptian killed was a woman, not a man. ___ Frankel and Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington, Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut and Omar Albam in Maarat al-Numan, Syria, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/missile-attack-airport-saudi-arabias-072026942.html

item.title: Republicans want Abdul El-Sayed to be the main character of the midterms. He's on board.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed , holding a handheld mic and wearing his signature V-neck black shirt, slowly shook his head as a woman at his town hall described how she burned through her savings after undergoing emergency brain surgery. “I’m really sorry for your experience, and I hope that you’re on the mend,” said El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, after outlining proposals for guaranteed health care and paid leave. Later that night, while talking to reporters in the basement below the theatre, his tone was far different. El-Sayed called his Republican opponent Mike Rogers a “coward,” said President Donald Trump was “afraid” to visit the state and dismissed as “dumb” a question about whether Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States. The exchanges captured two sides of a candidate who is the central figure in one of the nation’s most consequential Senate races . El-Sayed would be the country's first Muslim senator, and he's crisscrossing the state to counter a Republican effort, fueled by tens of millions of dollars, to portray him as a dangerous radical. But he has also embraced his confrontational side by mocking and taunting Trump and Rogers. “If they want to make me the main character in the midterms, I’m not shying away from it,” El-Sayed said in an interview. “Run against me. See how well that works out for you.” El-Sayed’s brash, swaggering confidence rubbed some Democrats the wrong way during a divisive primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. The former public health official has shown little interest in toning it down, remaining unapologetic about his progressive agenda and adversarial approach, emboldening supporters who believe he's the right candidate for an angry electorate that has lost faith in the political establishment. But his doubters fear he'll cost Democrats control of the Senate by failing to unite his party's disparate factions ahead of November. “If you want their votes, you have to make nice with those people, and he’s not really doing that,” said Michigan political strategist Adrian Hemond, who supported Stevens. “Maybe he doesn’t have to. The entire theory of this candidacy has been he can remake what the electorate looks like.” Republicans target El-Sayed Even though Michigan backed Trump twice in his three presidential campaigns, no Republican has won a Senate race in the state since 1994. The political landscape is no friendlier this year . Trump started an unpopular war with Iran, leading to higher gas prices. Rogers has opted for a low-key campaign with fewer public events than El-Sayed as he tries to make the race all about his Democratic opponent. As of Oct. 10, Republicans had outspent Democrats by $78 million to $63 million in the Michigan Senate race, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. Around $40 million in Republican spending has gone toward negative advertisements, compared to only around $20 million from Democrats. The ads portray El-Sayed as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme,” highlighting his past calls to defund the police and relax immigration enforcement. Others tie him to Hasan Piker, a popular online streamer with whom El-Sayed has appeared and who has drawn criticism for past comments, including saying that “America deserved 9/11.” On Friday, Rogers appeared alongside Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy, who told reporters that El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey.” Rogers laughed. Vice President JD Vance has called him “evil.” In one social media post, Trump shared a photo of himself with first lady Melania Trump alongside a photo of El-Sayed and his wife, who wears a hijab, with the caption: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.” Late Wednesday, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and said he “goes back to the days of the Jihad.” El-Sayed has hardly backed down. At the campaign stop in Port Huron, he taunted Trump to visit Michigan, suggesting Rogers and other Republicans were afraid the president would hurt their chances. “Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man,” El-Sayed said. And he responded to Kennedy’s attack by suggesting the Republican is in the KKK. “That’s rich coming from someone who wears his bed sheets out at night,” El-Sayed posted on social media. El-Sayed uses a personal touch with voters Before the Port Huron town hall, El-Sayed worked his way down a line of people who couldn’t fit inside the theater, shaking hands, taking photos and stopping for conversations. Jeff Petrucella and his wife Alice traveled from Macomb County to see El-Sayed. They described themselves as politically “middle of the road” and said they had voted Republican in the past. “I’m pretty done with the Republicans right now,” Jeff said. Alice said she was “looking for a change that is better for my granddaughters,” pointing to El-Sayed’s support for Medicare for All. Nor was she put off by his more confrontational appearances on Fox News. “I think he expresses himself well. You can tell he’s a well-spoken, educated man,” she said. Pat Kreiner was among those who waited nearly an hour to see El-Sayed. Her children had persuaded her to support him in the Democratic primary. “My son said to me, ‘I have been living with this trickle-down economy since the day I was born,’” Kreiner said. “‘It doesn’t work for me.’” Kreiner also expressed anger about Trump's trade war with Canada, just across the river from Port Huron. “We are heartsick about our neighbors,” she said. “They used to come over a lot. We don’t see them now.” Visiting smaller towns such as Port Huron has become central to El-Sayed’s campaign, with his team recently saying he's held more than 500 events in over 100 cities across the state. “Go everywhere. Talk to everyone. That’s what we do,” El-Sayed said in an interview. The personal approach has not erased all the skepticism surrounding El-Sayed, including within his own party. His criticism of Israel and association with Piker have raised concerns among some Jewish Democrats. El-Sayed has held a series of private gatherings with undecided Jewish voters as he works to win their support. He has also sought to strengthen his standing with Black voters. In the Democratic primary, Stevens drew more support in Wayne County, home to Detroit and its large Black population. Ahead of Thursday’s debate, El-Sayed attended two events with Black leaders before stopping at a Black barbershop, where he moved from chair to chair talking with customers. He stopped at one point to speak with a pregnant woman, congratulating her and asking when her baby was due. “November 8th?” El-Sayed joked. “Make sure you vote early, huh?” The race has become about more than just Michigan While El-Sayed has spent much of his campaign trying to win over Michigan voters, his candidacy has taken on significance far beyond the state. Republicans have made him a symbol of what they warn is an increasingly radical Democratic Party, while progressives see his campaign as a chance to prove their politics can win in a closely divided state. At a New York City fundraiser on Oct. 5, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez cast his campaign as a test for progressives nationwide. “If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” said the New York Democrat, a potential presidential candidate. Ocasio-Cortez plans to campaign with El-Sayed in Michigan next week, followed by former President Barack Obama on Oct. 24 . The national stakes have also drawn renewed opposition. United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with AIPAC, disclosed an initial $94,000 expenditure against El-Sayed on Friday, after spending nearly $30 million to oppose him in the Democratic primary. And El-Sayed, despite insisting the election should focus on Michigan voters and their economic struggles, has embraced the larger implications of his candidacy. “I am grateful for your support,” he told the audience at the New York fundraiser, according to remarks obtained by The Associated Press. He said he had two goals — “pick up a U.S. Senate seat” and “change the nature of our politics for the better.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republicans-want-abdul-el-sayed-112552011.html

item.title: He shares a name with a Cornell rape suspect. Strangers started hunting him down.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The messages told him he should “rot in hell” and be thrown in jail. His friends and family received a barrage of menacing threats. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Strangers found his cellphone number and peppered his phone with abusive texts. His face was plastered across angry videos online. Even TMZ called him. The messengers had wrongly concluded that the man was one of the seven Chi Phi fraternity members accused of participating in a 2024 gang rape at Cornell University, a case that has commanded public attention since the accuser, known as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit last month. But the man, a graduate student in engineering at the University of Pennsylvania, never attended Cornell - he merely shares a first and last name with one of the accused men. To make matters clear, he recently changed his LinkedIn bio to read, “I do NOT go to Cornell.” As the Cornell case has fueled public debate, it has inspired a frenzy of online sleuths, who are racing to identify and expose personal information about Jane Doe and the men she has accused, a phenomenon called “doxing.” Since Jane Doe filed the lawsuit, she has faced death threats and been confronted at her home by armed police after someone made a false report, an action called swatting, according to Thomas Giuffra, her attorney. In their rush, the digital vigilantes have made errors - falsely identifying a slew of people who are not connected to the case. At least three other women have been misidentified as Jane Doe on social media, Giuffra said, prompting a wave of videos in which women declare, “I am Jane Doe,” to show solidarity with the accuser and attempt to obscure her identity. After the home address of a Marine Corps sergeant who shares a name with one of the accused was mistakenly added to court documents, his family received threats, said John Manly, an attorney representing his family. The error led the New York Supreme Court judge handling the case to seal several court documents Friday and to condemn the harassment as “brash, reckless, and ultimately dangerous internet vigilantism.” The Penn grad student said he has been worried that online vigilantes might find his home address, adding that “overall, the past few weeks have taken a toll on my mental health.” The men accused in the Cornell case have not been charged, and The Washington Post is not naming them. One man who shares a name with one of the accused, and who graduated from Cornell four years before the incident, posted a video showing messages he had received. “You can’t hide. Your future is over. You’ll get exactly what you deserve, which is prison,” one said. In another video, he read a message from a woman claiming to be a witch who said she placed a hex on him: “Your soul will not find peace for the rest of your life,” she had told him. The Marine sergeant’s mother said she and her family have been “absolutely terrorized with threats.” She said her son has received a torrent of hateful messages through social media, while she and her daughter have received phone calls and text messages, including in the middle of the night. One person said, “I will find you.” Another said, “Rope is cheap and gravity is free.” The mother said that they’ve tried to tell people they had the wrong person, but that people just called them liars. People have also thrown garbage and unidentified substances in their yard, she said, including what looked like dog poop. She said it has been hard for the family to sleep. “We really - I can’t stress this enough - we really want to be left alone.” For years, online sleuths have misidentified the subjects of high-profile news events, according to University of Michigan professor Sarita Schoenebeck, who studies online harassment. A Brown University student who had been missing when pressure-cooker bombs detonated near the Boston Marathon finish line in 2013 was falsely named as the bomber by online sleuths. He had died by suicide a month before the bombing, but he was elevated as a possible suspect in the fallout. Schoenebeck said the damage to people named by mistake can persist long after people point out the errors. “Once misinformation spreads, corrections rarely reach as many people as the original claims,” she said. There are few reliable statistics on the frequency of doxing, but Schoenebeck said people turn to such methods when “they believe the justice system has failed. However, doxing itself lacks the fact-finding, safeguards and accountability that an effective justice system requires.” There is no comprehensive national law that prohibits posting someone’s personal information. Some states bar people from publishing addresses or other information with the intent to harass or harm someone. A federal law also makes it a crime to share sensitive information about certain federal officials, jurors and others to threaten, intimidate or incite violence. Some bystanders have targeted people more distantly connected to the Cornell case. While at least two websites feature the names and photos of the accused, a longer list of fraternity members has also appeared online. “It wasn’t just seven. 50 other individuals knew what was happening and did NOTHING,” one post on Facebook reads. It includes pictures of Chi Phi fraternity members. Some of the online posts have included former members who graduated before the incident and were not part of a group chat involving the accused, and who are now facing harassment, their attorney, Adam Ford, wrote to Cornell’s general counsel in a letter reviewed by The Post. Ford said his clients have received death threats and hate mail, with some facing adverse consequences from their universities and employers, such as being put on leave. These alumni “had nothing to do with the events surrounding Jane Doe,” Ford wrote in the letter. “Nevertheless, they are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement.” The letter was first reported by CBS News. In his letter, Ford asked Cornell to provide letters to the alumni verifying that they were not part of the incident and to call on the public to stop harassing current and former members of the fraternity. Cornell declined to comment on the letter to The Post, citing pending litigation. The Penn student said he understands the human impulse to seek justice. “I salute those who are willing and strong enough to take matters into their own hands, especially when large organizations and institutions take too long to address an issue,” he told The Post. However, he said that his case demonstrates that it’s more important than ever to fact-check sources and verify information. “Mob mentality is real, and it can spread just as easily on social media,” he said. “People just need to be mindful of the impact our words and actions can have.” CORRECTION: A man who shares a name with one of the accused posted a video saying he graduated from Cornell four years before the incident. An earlier version of this article mistakenly said it was two years prior. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/11/how-cornell-rape-case-turned-into-sprawling-campaign-harassment/

item.title: Next steps in the Cornell sexual assault case — and the challenges that lie ahead
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has tapped Attorney General Letitia James (right) to be the special prosecutor in the Cornell University sexual assault case. They attended a press conference on October 2 in New York. - NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/AP When New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James to take over the investigation into an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University, she asked for a “fresh and thorough” review of all the evidence. And there is a lot of evidence. Far from the two-party “he said-she said” structure of many sexual assault allegations, the Cornell case features seven men accused of wrongdoing in a civil suit filed by the woman known as Jane Doe. There are interviews with Doe, the accused men and other witnesses ; scores of texts and Snapchat posts ; secretly recorded phone calls ; and lengthy, conflicting reports from the police, district attorney and university investigators about who knew what when. In all, it’s a far cry from the limited evidence the local prosecutor said he reviewed before deciding not to bring charges in 2024. Putting the array of evidence together represents the primary task ahead for James, the special prosecutor tasked with leading the investigation and considering whether to bring charges. How the investigation proceeds will be closely watched by community members, university students and advocacy groups across the country. “There is literally an avalanche of statements to collect in this case that apparently were not reviewed by the original prosecutor,” said Paul DerOhannesian, an Albany-based attorney and author of “Sexual Assault Trials.” “Getting all those statements is a big task,” he said. Mimi Rocah, former Westchester County district attorney and former federal prosecutor, likened the work ahead to “putting the pieces of the puzzle together.” Hochul laid out the questions James will try to answer in a news conference on October 2. “Attorney General James will be the one who puts a spotlight on this case and says, ‘Who knew what when?’ ‘What did they do wrong?’ ‘Why didn’t they come forward?’ and ‘How was this woman denied justice?’ and we anticipate that will come out over the right period of time,” Hochul said. For James, the investigation faces several key challenges ahead, including the potential loss of evidence two years after the fact, questions about her potential bias, a supposed “loophole” in New York’s sexual assault law and intense pressure from the community. The most important job of a special prosecutor, Rocah said, is “to try to conduct a fair process and really convey that to the public and be transparent at the end of the day about what you did and why you did it.” The immediate next steps for James At the news conference, James laid out her next steps as special prosecutor. “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard,” she said. “We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions.” unknown content item - Much of the evidence may already exist. Notably, Cornell held its own formal Title IX investigation, the federal civil rights law banning discrimination based on gender – which includes sexual harassment and violence. The investigation included more than 50 interviews, including with all of the men accused of wrongdoing, except one who declined to be interviewed, according to a heavily redacted 99-page document summarizing the panel’s findings. CNN has not seen the Title IX filings, which are generally confidential and restricted to the parties involved. Separately, Cornell is reviewing its own response to the sexual assault allegations. This review, led by former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates, will examine how Cornell “prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus,” the university said . Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York. - Surya Vaidy/CNN Still, James will have the opportunity to reinterview certain witnesses rather than simply relying on previous evidence. DerOhannesian said James will have a few extra tools at her disposal in this investigation. She could try to cut a deal with some of the accused, offering leniency or immunity in exchange for their testimony. Or she could try to look for evidence of process crimes, such as obstruction of justice or lying to investigators, if the evidence allows. Her role here as special prosecutor is not so different from how prosecutors may reexamine cases started by their predecessors. “That is not uncommon for people in decision-making positions to have to take a look at past investigations and past decisions,” Rocah said. With so much ahead, the investigation is likely to take a while, DerOhannesian said. “Because of the quantity of information that has to be processed, the multiple legal questions that have to be answered for multiple individuals, I think it’s gonna take a lot of time,” he said. “That may be frustrating to the community, that it will be taking time to get these answers.” The office has reached out to several experienced attorneys to bolster its team, CNN reported Tuesday . The attorney general’s office, known as OAG, “has spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation. The DA has agreed to cooperate, and OAG remains committed to a thorough and independent investigation guided only by the facts and the law,” a spokesperson for James said in a statement. Once the investigation is complete, James likely will either take her findings to a grand jury or issue a report explaining why she does not recommend charges. The challenges ahead for James One challenge for James is some evidence may have been lost in the two years since the October 2024 encounter. Memories may have faded, or digital evidence could have been lost or deleted. “There are real challenges looking at something several years after it happened,” Rocah said. Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said her rape kit was conducted weeks after the incident rather than immediately afterward, potentially losing some DNA evidence. He also speculated that photos and videos of the incident may have been lost or deleted due to the failures of the original investigation. “I mean, if this was a normal investigation that was done in New York City, for example, they would have gotten search warrants,” Giuffra told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Monday. They would have grabbed every single one of these phones of these guys. They would have downloaded all this material. Another challenge for James is convincing the public to trust her independence and judgment. Late last month, she posted about Doe’s case, calling her a “survivor” and declaring, “We stand with you.” Days later, at the news conference announcing her appointment as special prosecutor, she declined to comment on the post. Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for one of the seven former fraternity members, on Monday called for James to recuse herself from the case, saying her statements “could reasonably be understood as accepting that the alleged conduct occurred before she assumed responsibility for determining what the evidence establishes.” Finally, any criminal charges would have to follow New York’s law defining sex crimes and lack of consent. In particular, lack of consent can result from being involuntarily “mentally incapacitated” by drugs or alcohol. But if someone voluntarily takes drugs or alcohol, they can’t be considered mentally incapacitated – an exclusion critics have called a “ loophole .” In Doe’s case, she has said she drank alcohol and took drugs that night. She also told police she was OK with an initial encounter but said she did not consent to sexual contact later in the night, according to a six-page statement obtained by CNN. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited this law and Doe’s alcohol and drug use in defending his decision not to charge the accused fraternity members. However, he acknowledged he did not see all the evidence in the case before coming to that conclusion. Giuffra said Doe’s reactions to the incident were a “textbook reaction to trauma.” “Ms. Doe’s internal processing went from denial to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends,” Giuffra told CNN Thursday. This aspect of New York law will make bringing charges a “tough climb” for prosecutors, said CNN senior legal analyst Elie Honig. Still, investigators could bring charges here under different theories, legal experts said. Even when someone consumes drugs or alcohol, they still may not be able to consent, or they could offer consent at one time and revoke it later, DerOhannesian said. It all depends on the specific facts of the case, Rocah said. “It makes a case under facts like this more challenging, but not impossible,” she said. CNN’s Kara Scannell contributed to this report. item.title: Ozempic or retirement? Some users are sacrificing savings to pay for prescriptions.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Americans taking popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound may be facing a new financial dilemma: save for retirement or pay for the drugs helping improve their health. A new survey from the Nationwide Retirement Institute found that 51% of current GLP-1 users worry they may have to choose between medication costs and retirement savings. The survey suggests those concerns are already affecting financial decisions. According to Nationwide, 54% of current users have changed their financial behavior to afford the medications, including 17% who have taken on debt, 14% who have withdrawn money from savings or retirement accounts and 14% who have reduced retirement contributions. Counterfeit Ozempic scheme traced to China, feds say Out-of-pocket costs remain a major challenge, especially for patients whose insurance does not fully cover treatment. According to InvestmentNews , users without full coverage spend an average of $203 a month out of pocket, even as many expect to remain on the drugs long term to maintain weight-loss and metabolic benefits. Yet many users believe the health benefits may outweigh the financial sacrifice. The Nationwide survey found that 88% of current GLP-1 users are more optimistic about their long-term health, while 64% say they may retire later because they feel healthier. Nearly six in 10 respondents said improved health makes them feel less pressure to increase retirement savings. GLP-1 drugs linked to nutritional deficiencies in kids, study says Financial planners are increasingly grappling with questions that barely existed a few years ago, including whether clients should reduce retirement contributions to afford GLP-1 medications and whether improved health today could offset future healthcare costs. Kristi Martin Rodriguez of the Nationwide Retirement Institute said rising GLP-1 use is creating new financial planning challenges. "If what you're spending on your health today is competing with what you're saving for tomorrow, that needs to be part of the financial planning conversation," Rodriguez said. The findings underscore a broader affordability challenge as demand for GLP-1 drugs continues to soar. While insurers and some employers have expanded coverage for obesity and diabetes treatments, many Americans still face substantial out-of-pocket expenses. According to Nationwide, 59% of current users worry about being able to afford GLP-1 medications in retirement, raising the prospect that these drugs could become a major retirement-planning issue in the years ahead.
